title: Greetings
sourceNote: The auto-captions garble most German words; all greetings were reconstructed from context and standard German. The teacher says he will explain the endings in 'Guten' / 'Gute' in a later video.
objectives: I can greet people in German at different times of the day
I can say goodbye formally and informally
I can recognise regional greetings such as Grüß Gott and Servus
I can pronounce ß and understand the basic sound of the umlaut ü

expressions.en: Hello! (the most common greeting; pronounced 'hallo', not 'hello')
Hi! (very informal, used by some people)
Good day! / Hello! (mostly formal; any time of day)
Good evening! (also fine late in the evening)
Good night! (said before going to bed)
Hello! (casual, to one friend or known person)
Hello! / Bye! (southern Germany, Austria; any time of day)
Goodbye! (on the phone, when you cannot see the person)
See you later! (alternative to Bis bald)

grammar.title: Formal and informal greetings
grammar.body:
German has two ways of addressing a person: **Sie** (formal, for strangers, officials, older people) and **du** (informal, for friends, family, children). You see this already in two regional greetings:

**Grüß Sie!** is formal and **Grüß dich!** is casual. Both are used only for ONE person. For a group you cannot use them.

**Guten Tag** (used during the day) and **Auf Wiedersehen** sound formal; **Guten Abend** is the formal evening greeting. **Hallo**, **Tschüs** and **Bis bald** sound informal.
grammar.ar: Sie للمخاطب الرسمي، وdu للأصدقاء والعائلة.

grammar.title: Guten or Gute?
grammar.body: Notice that **Guten** Tag, **Guten** Morgen and **Guten** Abend end in **-n**, but **Gute** Nacht does not. The teacher asks you not to worry about the reason yet: just learn the four greetings as fixed phrases. The reason is explained in later lessons.

mistakes.why: The German word is spelled with *a* and pronounced 'hallo'.
Morning, day and evening all take *Guten*; only *Nacht* takes *Gute*.
*Gute Nacht* is a fixed phrase without -n.

pronunciation.tip: This letter is called Eszett and sounds like a double s (ss). *Grüß*, *Grüß Gott*.
Make the lips round as for 'oo' but say 'ee'. *Grüß*, *Tschüs*.
Before a vowel s sounds like English z: *Servus* starts with a 'z' sound; *Sie* sounds like 'zee'.
When greeting in Germany, look the person in the eye and give a firm handshake.

tip: Repeat each greeting aloud several times. Pronunciation matters more than details at this stage: do not worry about the grammar yet.

comprehension.q: How do you say 'good evening' in German?
Which greeting do you say before going to bed?
Which goodbye do you use on the phone?
Which greeting is formal: Grüß Sie or Grüß dich?
In which German state is Grüß Gott mostly spoken?

exercises.title: Match the greetings
exercises.instructions: Match each German greeting with its English meaning.

exercises.title: Fill in the gap
exercises.instructions: Complete each greeting with one word.

exercises.title: Choose the right greeting
exercises.instructions: Choose the best greeting for the situation.

items.q: You say goodbye on the phone. (Auf Wiedersehen / Auf Wiederhören)
items.expl: On the phone you cannot see the person, so you 'hear' them again.

items.q: You greet one friend casually. (Grüß dich / Grüß Sie)
You greet a stranger formally at any time of day. (Guten Tag / Gute Nacht)
items.expl: *Gute Nacht* is only for going to bed.

items.q: You leave a friend you will see later. (Bis später / Guten Abend)
You say goodnight to your family. (Gute Nacht / Guten Morgen)
Say 'Good day!' (formal, any time of day).
Say 'Hello' in the way people greet in Bavaria and Austria (with God).

summary: Hallo is the most common greeting for any time of day. Guten Tag is more formal and used during the day. Guten Abend is for the evening.
Use Guten Morgen, Guten Abend and Gute Nacht for specific times of day.
Regional greetings: Grüß Gott, Grüß dich / Grüß Sie, Servus. Informal goodbyes: Tschüs, Ciao, Bis bald, Bis später.
Auf Wiedersehen is the formal goodbye; Auf Wiederhören is used on the phone.
ß sounds like ss, and ü is a rounded 'ee' sound.
